short: A flogged queen led a British uprising that burned three Roman cities to the ground.
full:
In 60 or 61 CE, Roman officials seized the kingdom of the Iceni on the death of client king Prasutagus, flogged his widow Boudica and assaulted their daughters. With the governor Suetonius Paulinus campaigning in Anglesey, Boudica led the Iceni and Trinovantes in revolt, sacking Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium and killing, according to Roman accounts, tens of thousands of Roman citizens and allies.

Suetonius Paulinus regrouped his available forces and met the much larger British army at an unlocated site, likely along Watling Street. Disciplined Roman infantry, funnelled by the terrain, broke the British ranks and inflicted catastrophic casualties; Boudica died shortly afterward, by poison according to Tacitus. The revolt very nearly forced Rome to abandon Britain altogether, and its brutality prompted an inquiry into provincial administration that replaced the procurator responsible for the original outrage.
